guide_sections.heading: Trace the two update stories
guide_sections.body:
The worked examples make the same kind of assignment and get opposite results. Tracing each binding step by step shows where they diverge.

```text
step            x          y          identical(x, y)
y <- x          A=1 B=2    A=1 B=2    TRUE
y[[1]] <- 99    A=1 B=2    A=99 B=2   FALSE
```

The vector update gives y its own copy at the moment it is modified, so x keeps 1.

```text
step                first$count  second$count
first$count <- 1    1            1
second <- first     1            1
second$count <- 2   2            2
```

The environment is never copied. `second <- first` gives a second name to the same object, so the update is visible through both names. In the starter, `print(attributes(original))` shows a single `$names` entry holding "A" and "B"; after `unname()` the same call prints NULL, which is the quickest way to confirm that a step removed metadata.

exercises.approach: Run the assignment and the update, then inspect both vectors.
exercises.why: R vectors follow copy-on-modify semantics: `y <- x` shares the data until `y[1] <- 9` changes y, at which point y gets its own copy. x still holds A = 1 and B = 2.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the edit to show through x because both names once referred to the same object. That is how the environment in Example 2 behaves, not an ordinary numeric vector.
exercises.verify: The reference check `x[[1]] == 1` passes, and `y[[1]]` returns 9.

exercises.approach: Call `unname(x)` and compare the result with the bare values.
exercises.why: `unname` removes only the names attribute. The values 1 and 2 are untouched, so the result is identical to `c(1, 2)`.
exercises.wrong: Writing `names(x) <- ""`. That assigns one empty name and pads the second with NA, so the object still has a names attribute and is not identical to `c(1, 2)`.
exercises.verify: `is.null(names(z))` returns TRUE and `identical(z, c(1, 2))` is TRUE, as the reference asserts.

exercises.approach: Set `dim(m) <- c(2L, 2L)` on the four values from `1:4`.
exercises.why: Two rows times two columns is four cells, exactly the vector length. R fills by column, so the first column is 1, 2 and the second is 3, 4.
exercises.wrong: Requesting `c(3L, 2L)` fails because six cells do not match four values. Expecting row filling, with 1 and 2 across the top row, misreads every later position.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `identical(dim(m), c(2L, 2L))`, and `m[1, 2]` returns 3.

exercises.approach: Recognize that `alias <- e` gives a second name to one environment, then create a separate `new.env()` when independent state is needed.
exercises.why: An environment is a reference object. Setting `alias$count <- 3` changes the only count that exists, so `e$count` becomes 3 as well.
exercises.wrong: Expecting `alias <- e` to copy the way `y <- x` copied a vector, and then debugging an unexpected count somewhere else in the script.
exercises.verify: In the reference, `e$count` returns 3 after the alias update, and `identical(e, alias)` is TRUE.

exercises.approach: Use `identical()` for exact object equality and compare the attributes as well as the values.
exercises.why: `c(A = 1)` carries a names attribute that 1 lacks, so the two objects differ even though their single value matches.
exercises.wrong: Concluding that the values differ, or using `==` where identity was required. `c(A = 1) == 1` returns TRUE with the name A attached, hiding the metadata difference.
exercises.verify: `attributes(c(A = 1))` shows a `$names` entry, while `attributes(1)` returns NULL.

exercises.approach: Write the contract as explicit checks on names, dimensions and class, not only on values.
exercises.why: In this lesson the names A and B carry record identity, and Example 3 shows how a single-column selection can drop dim without changing any value.
exercises.wrong: Testing only `all(result == c(1, 2))`. That passes after `unname()` or `as.numeric()` has stripped the labels a caller relies on.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `identical(names(x), c("A", "B"))`, a test that fails as soon as the labels change.
